crm-s › components › siebel › name: Siebel ICM
crm-s › components › siebel › short: The current system, until switched off
crm-s › components › siebel › what: ICM, the current case management system, built on Oracle Siebel and running on government servers.
crm-s › components › siebel › does: It keeps running for programs not yet moved, and shares data with the CRM platform through the connector.
crm-s › components › siebel › why: Switching off ICM too early would leave staff without records. Running both costs money, so a clear end date matters.
crm-s › components › siebel › buildBuy › label: Existing: runs until it is retired
crm-s › components › siebel › buildBuy › summary: Siebel stays in place during the move and is shut down once every program is on the CRM platform.

=== src/lib/content/event-driven.yaml
event-driven › name: Event-driven
event-driven › nickname: Built in parts
event-driven › tagline: Smaller replaceable parts linked by messages. Reuse or buy common parts; build what is unique to BC.
event-driven › summary › 1: This design was devised over several years including extensive field research, interviews, landscape analyses and other research. Instead of a single tightly integrated monolith, it is a set of smaller parts. Each part does one job, keeps its own records and belongs to a team. Common components can be adopted, like authentication, email, printing, or document intelligence or made available like the event-broker, business rules engine, or orchestration service. CSBC builds only the parts that are unique to business' programs, such as eligibility rules and the management of determination of facts from claims and evidence, or process handling for the hundreds of exceptions, edge-cases and carve outs.
event-driven › summary › 2: The parts talk to each other through events. An event is a short message that says something happened, like "a client submitted a monthly report" or "a payment was approved". Any part that cares can listen and act. Because no part reaches into another part's records, one part can be replaced without breaking the rest.
event-driven › summary › 3: The new parts are switched on one area at a time, while ICM keeps running. A bridge into ICM lets old and new work side by side until each piece of ICM can be turned off.
event-driven › facts › 1 › label: Labour effort
event-driven › facts › 1 › value: 680 labour-months, in a range of 560 to 750.
event-driven › facts › 2 › label: Time to initial value
event-driven › facts › 2 › value: 6-10 months.
event-driven › facts › 3 › label: Clear Win
event-driven › facts › 3 › value: Notices, letters, forms and data validation can be implemented quickly and will immediately benefit ICM and be usable in future systems.
event-driven › facts › 4 › label: Build vs. Buy
event-driven › facts › 4 › value: Mostly mature, well-supported open source products, many with commercial support. Build is focused on high-impact, mission critical components.
event-driven › goodAt › 1: Each element can be modified or replaced independently, so there is no vendor lock-in or software stack monopoly. These components can be re-used by other projects or spun out into common components.
event-driven › goodAt › 2: Every element is captured as structured data, including the claims, evidence, rules and processes, so it can be tested, validated and automated.
event-driven › goodAt › 3: Policy staff can self-manage rates, and business rules through a tested release process and a tool set they've already validated. No technician, no waiting for release.
event-driven › goodAt › 4: ICM is replaced incrementally, with many features benefiting both the new system and ICM, and no "big bang."
event-driven › goodAt › 5: Sensitive data and critical processes stay on the Province's own servers using trustworthy software.
event-driven › goodAt › 6: Several components are already built or under way - a workflow orchestration system (Airflow in CriDIR), a business rules management system (BRE), a data integration gateway (EFV in DMI), a UX construction framework (MySS rebuild), a real-time data processing system and data lake (Spark, CriDIR), an anti-corruption layer for seamless migration (ICM-API)
event-driven › goodAt › 7: Business areas were invested in and support of an event-driven architecture
event-driven › goodAt › 8: Maximizing in-sourcing and internal knowledge development
event-driven › goodAt › 9: Designed for AI from the ground up, every facet of the system can leverage AI tools now or in the future.
event-driven › watchOut › 1: Many of the design commitments may be unfamiliar or unintuitive (e.g. there is no "CRM")
event-driven › watchOut › 2: Initial development will focus on establishing a "kit" of capabilities, while they can be demonstrated they do not provide the immediate gratification of a commercial CRM tool.
event-driven › watchOut › 3: Because there is no cut-over, both systems will run side-by-side for a time. Some improvements can be back-migrated to ICM, this may seem like wasted investment, but the timelines warrant it.
event-driven › watchOut › 4: CSBC, or those it hires, must build and run several elements itself. It needs a stable, capable team.
event-driven › watchOut › 5: Engineering discipline must be maintained as part of team culture, rather than enforced by the system itself, e.g. the event log can be misused, resulting in the tangled, tightly coupled mess of ICM.
event-driven › zones › 1 › name: Unified user experience
event-driven › zones › 1 › blurb: AI-augmented from day 1. The screens and workflows people use, tailored to suit their context using an ever-growing library of smart components.
event-driven › zones › 2 › name: Service abstraction layer
event-driven › zones › 2 › blurb: An easy to use API layer for application authors (and AI) to construct service experiences. Frees developers and services designers from back-end implementation considerations. Allows back-end developers to make changes without disturbing the UX. These can be assembled very quickly by AI
event-driven › zones › 3 › name: Domain capabilities
event-driven › zones › 3 › blurb: These domain capabilities encapsulate the elements of the system that are unique and high-value. By keeping them contained, this prevents commodity boilerplate from creeping in. These can be built by different teams in a polyglot environment and are easy for AI to reliably engineer.
event-driven › zones › 4 › name: Service intelligence
event-driven › zones › 4 › blurb: These components allow the system to react adaptively to changes through orchestration and agents.
event-driven › zones › 5 › name: Event broker
event-driven › zones › 5 › blurb: The message line that carries news of every change from one part to the others.
event-driven › zones › 6 › name: Commodity components
event-driven › zones › 6 › blurb: Common tools every large organisation needs. These are reused from government, adopted as free software or bought, not built.
event-driven › zones › 7 › name: Links to other systems
event-driven › zones › 7 › blurb: Bridges to other organisations, and to ICM while old and new run side by side.
event-driven › components › worker-context › name: Worker Experiences
event-driven › components › worker-context › short: What caseworkers and contact centre staff use
event-driven › components › worker-context › what: The workflows, wizards, and agents ministry staff use daily. Caseworkers, supervisors, and contact centre staff each have tailored experiences for maximized ergonomics.
event-driven › components › worker-context › does: Surfaces a client's context, aids in discovering necessary information, ensuring service quality and managing tasks. Staff fulfill processes, act on work queues and access reports and information. The UX is self-explaining where it is not self-evident, accessible and multi-modal.
event-driven › components › worker-context › why: Staff must manage dozens of generic screens with workflows scattered and disorder among them. UX tools built around the specific needs for their tasks saves time and improves data and serve quality. The combination of component libraries, automated tests, and AI tooling makes designing, building, validating and testing these very fast and very cheap.
event-driven › components › worker-context › buildBuy › label: Build from a shared library of smart components
event-driven › components › worker-context › buildBuy › summary: The design builds experiences from a common library of smart components built atop the GovBC design system. Smart components are not just UI widgets, they come pre-wired with the data to make them usable. AI tools like Copilot can be provided skills or specialized agents to construct experiences through chat. Developers can also use AI to develop new components to add to the library. Rather than devolving into a junk drawer of gadgets, AI can both contend with tens of thousands of components easily and provide mechanisms for curation, deduplication, refactoring etc.
event-driven › components › worker-context › buildBuy › options › 1 › name: Shared library of smart components
event-driven › components › worker-context › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: Accessibility is designed in, not applied later. Full experiences, not just UI widgets.
event-driven › components › worker-context › buildBuy › options › 2 › name: Provincial design system
event-driven › components › worker-context › buildBuy › options › 2 › note: Provides a kernel for expansion as new UI elements are developed.
event-driven › components › worker-context › buildBuy › options › 3 › name: Case platform screens (a SaaS CRM, Dynamics 365, Pega, Appian)
event-driven › components › worker-context › buildBuy › options › 3 › note: Not recommended. Full price for a sliver of the product, underlying model doesn't map well to new system.
event-driven › components › client-context › name: Client Experiences
event-driven › components › client-context › short: What people already receiving help use
event-driven › components › client-context › what: The online screens for people already receiving assistance or services, and for those acting on their behalf.
event-driven › components › client-context › does: Lets clients report changes, upload documents, read their notices and see their payments. Anything they can do online can also be done by phone, in person or on paper.
event-driven › components › client-context › why: Many clients cannot easily use a website. The design says no right or deadline can be online only, so clients get the same result whichever way they reach the ministry.
event-driven › components › client-context › buildBuy › label: Build from the shared library of screen parts
event-driven › components › client-context › buildBuy › summary: Client screens use the same shared building blocks as the worker screens. They reach the system through the same doorway, so they keep working as parts behind it are replaced. No product comparison has been done for client screens.
event-driven › components › client-context › buildBuy › options › 1 › name: Shared library of screen parts
event-driven › components › client-context › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: Same blocks as the worker screens.
event-driven › components › client-context › buildBuy › options › 2 › name: Provincial design system
event-driven › components › client-context › buildBuy › options › 2 › note: Used where it fits, behind the ministry's library.
event-driven › components › applicant-context › name: Applicant screens
event-driven › components › applicant-context › short: Where people apply for help
event-driven › components › applicant-context › what: The screens for people applying for the first time, on their own or with help from a worker or agency.
event-driven › components › applicant-context › does: Takes an application, collects the facts and documents needed, and starts the eligibility check. A worker can complete an application on someone's behalf, and the system records who did it.
event-driven › components › applicant-context › why: Applying is the first contact many people have with the ministry, often at a hard moment. A clear application with no lost paperwork means faster decisions and fewer repeat visits.
event-driven › components › applicant-context › buildBuy › label: Build from the shared library of screen parts
event-driven › components › applicant-context › buildBuy › summary: Built with the same shared building blocks as the other screens. No product comparison has been done for application screens.
event-driven › components › applicant-context › buildBuy › options › 1 › name: Shared library of screen parts
event-driven › components › applicant-context › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: Same blocks as the other screens.
event-driven › components › applicant-context › buildBuy › options › 2 › name: Provincial design system
event-driven › components › applicant-context › buildBuy › options › 2 › note: Used where it fits.
event-driven › components › vendor-context › name: Partner and vendor screens
event-driven › components › vendor-context › short: What service providers and partners use
event-driven › components › vendor-context › what: The screens and connections for outside organisations, such as service providers, contracted agencies and other partners.
event-driven › components › vendor-context › does: Lets partners see referrals and service agreements, report on services delivered, and send or receive information the law allows them to share.
event-driven › components › vendor-context › why: Partners do much of the hands-on work for clients. Giving them their own access, limited to what an agreement allows, cuts phone calls and paper and protects client privacy.
event-driven › components › vendor-context › buildBuy › label: Build from the shared library of screen parts
event-driven › components › vendor-context › buildBuy › summary: Built with the same building blocks as the other screens. What each partner may see is set by information-sharing agreements held in a register, not granted by hand. No product comparison has been done for partner screens.
event-driven › components › vendor-context › buildBuy › options › 1 › name: Shared library of screen parts
event-driven › components › vendor-context › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: Same blocks as the other screens.
event-driven › components › service-layer › name: Service abstraction layer
event-driven › components › service-layer › short: One doorway into the system (APIs)
event-driven › components › service-layer › what: The single doorway that every screen, partner and report uses to reach the system. It is made of APIs. An API is a published, agreed way for one computer program to ask another for information or to get something done, a bit like a standard order form.
event-driven › components › service-layer › does: Takes each request, checks the person is allowed to make it, records it, and passes it to the right part. Behind it sit microservices: small programs that each do one job, like a counter that only handles one kind of request.
event-driven › components › service-layer › why: This doorway stays the same while the parts behind it change. Today some requests go to ICM; later the same requests go to new parts. Screens and partners do not have to change each time, which saves money and avoids disruption.
event-driven › components › service-layer › buildBuy › label: Build the doorway, reuse the Province's API tools
event-driven › components › service-layer › buildBuy › summary: The agreed request formats are the ministry's own and must outlive every part behind them, so they are designed and owned in-house. The design reuses the Province's API programme for the gateway software and directory. The research did not compare products for this part.
event-driven › components › service-layer › buildBuy › options › 1 › name: Ministry-owned request formats
event-driven › components › service-layer › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: Owned by the ministry, built to last longer than any one part.
event-driven › components › service-layer › buildBuy › options › 2 › name: Provincial API programme
event-driven › components › service-layer › buildBuy › options › 2 › note: Gateway and directory, reused.
event-driven › components › service-layer › watch › text: If ICM's own codes and record numbers leak into the doorway and a partner starts relying on them, the doorway can no longer outlive ICM. The design names this as its quietest risk and checks for it automatically.
event-driven › components › participant-identity › name: Participant identity
event-driven › components › participant-identity › short: Knowing two records are the same person
event-driven › components › participant-identity › what: A deliberately small part that holds the identifiers for each person the ministry serves, such as BC Services Card number and program numbers, and just enough detail to match records.
event-driven › components › participant-identity › does: Spots records that belong to the same person and sends uncertain matches to a staff member to decide. When records are merged or split, it tells every other part, and a wrong merge can be undone.
event-driven › components › participant-identity › why: ICM has many duplicate records and a search that only finds exact matches. Mixing up two people can mean wrong payments or a privacy breach. Getting identity right underpins everything else.
event-driven › components › participant-identity › buildBuy › label: Build a small service, adopt a matching library inside it
event-driven › components › participant-identity › buildBuy › summary: Matching names and dates is a common problem, so the research recommends adopting an existing matching library rather than writing one. The small service around it, with the review screen and undoable merges, is built. Products that hold a single master record of each client were ruled out, because that record would hold information that belongs to other parts.
event-driven › components › participant-identity › buildBuy › options › 1 › name: Splink, Zingg, dedupe
event-driven › components › participant-identity › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: Free matching libraries that run on the ministry's own servers.
event-driven › components › participant-identity › buildBuy › options › 2 › name: Senzing SDK
event-driven › components › participant-identity › buildBuy › options › 2 › note: Commercial matching library that runs on the ministry's own servers.
event-driven › components › participant-identity › buildBuy › options › 3 › name: Tamr, Reltio, Informatica, Semarchy
event-driven › components › participant-identity › buildBuy › options › 3 › note: Not recommended. They keep a master copy of each person.
event-driven › components › financial-components › name: Financial components
event-driven › components › financial-components › short: The ministry's record of money owed and paid
event-driven › components › financial-components › what: The ministry's own ledger for benefits: what each person is owed, what was paid, what was recovered and what was written off. The Province's corporate financial system stays the official book.
event-driven › components › financial-components › does: Turns each approved decision into a payment instruction. It checks its totals every day against the bank and the corporate financial system. It also tracks money paid now that may have to be repaid later, such as help while an appeal is decided.
event-driven › components › financial-components › why: This is where public money is accounted for. Clean daily checks catch errors before they reach clients, and keeping the ledger apart from the payment run means each can be audited on its own.
event-driven › components › financial-components › buildBuy › label: Build in the ministry's own database (proposed)
event-driven › components › financial-components › buildBuy › summary: A test compared a plain ledger table in the ministry's own database with three open-source ledger products. The plain table passed all nine tests, including posting a full monthly run of about 74,000 entries in under two seconds. No product did better. This direction is in a decision record that has not yet been accepted. How to check the ledger against the bank each day is still open, and suppliers may be asked to quote.
event-driven › components › financial-components › buildBuy › options › 1 › name: Ledger table in the ministry's own database
event-driven › components › financial-components › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: Proposed. Passed all nine tests, but it was one test.
event-driven › components › financial-components › buildBuy › options › 2 › name: TigerBeetle, Formance Ledger, Blnk Core
event-driven › components › financial-components › buildBuy › options › 2 › note: Not recommended. Each adds a second store, and two let the link to the decision be rewritten.
event-driven › components › financial-components › buildBuy › options › 3 › name: Apache Fineract, Kill Bill
event-driven › components › financial-components › buildBuy › options › 3 › note: Not recommended. They hold payments and debts together in one model.
event-driven › components › financial-components › buildBuy › options › 4 › name: Commercial reconciliation products
event-driven › components › financial-components › buildBuy › options › 4 › note: Not yet decided. Prices on request only.
event-driven › components › financial-components › watch › text: Provincial financial policy says ministries must use the Province's corporate financial systems where practical, and a new financial system needs the Comptroller General's approval. The research did not consider this, and the answer is not yet known.
event-driven › components › service-delivery › name: Service delivery
event-driven › components › service-delivery › short: Case work, one area per program
event-driven › components › service-delivery › what: The everyday case work, split into five separate areas: employment assistance, persons with disabilities, child care subsidy, employment services and child protection. Each has its own records and its own team.
event-driven › components › service-delivery › does: Handles applications, eligibility checks, supplements, service plans and case reviews for its program. Each area uses the shared parts for identity, evidence, rules, workflow and letters.
event-driven › components › service-delivery › why: Child protection and child care subsidy work very differently. Forcing them into one shared case model is what made ICM hard to change. Separate areas let each program improve without risking the others.
event-driven › components › service-delivery › buildBuy › label: Build (assemble on the shared parts)
event-driven › components › service-delivery › buildBuy › summary: The research recommends building the five program areas and not buying a case platform to hold the record. Platforms like a SaaS CRM, Dynamics 365, Pega and Appian keep only the current state of a case, not the full history of facts, and published licence prices for about 9,400 staff run from about CAD 49 to 164 million over three years before setup. An independent check later found Merative Cúram does keep that history, so this direction is now rated low in firmness.
event-driven › components › service-delivery › buildBuy › options › 1 › name: Five program areas built on shared parts
event-driven › components › service-delivery › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: Recommended, low firmness. Needs a funded team.
event-driven › components › service-delivery › buildBuy › options › 2 › name: Merative Cúram
event-driven › components › service-delivery › buildBuy › options › 2 › note: Meets the legal needs on current documents, but is one shared case model. A demonstration has been suggested.
event-driven › components › service-delivery › buildBuy › options › 3 › name: A SaaS CRM, Dynamics 365, Pega, Appian
event-driven › components › service-delivery › buildBuy › options › 3 › note: Not recommended as the record. Keep current state, not history.
event-driven › components › service-delivery › watch › text: The main reason for building was that no product keeps the history of facts. That does not hold for Cúram. A legal answer on what a tribunal needs, and a second look at the reasons for building, are needed before deciding.
event-driven › components › provider-outcome › name: Provider and outcome management
event-driven › components › provider-outcome › short: Service providers, placements and results
event-driven › components › provider-outcome › what: The part that manages outside services: facilities, placements, service agreements, referrals, plans and how well services worked.
event-driven › components › provider-outcome › does: Records which provider is authorised to deliver which service to whom, under what agreement, and tracks the results.
event-driven › components › provider-outcome › why: Much of the help clients get comes from contracted providers. Clear agreements and outcome tracking help the ministry pay the right providers and see which services actually help people.
event-driven › components › provider-outcome › buildBuy › label: Not yet analysed (default: build on the shared parts)
event-driven › components › provider-outcome › buildBuy › summary: No build-vs-buy analysis has been done for this part yet. The design treats it like the other program areas, with its own records and team. The sensible default is to build it on the shared parts, while checking whether a provider-management product could serve as its store without becoming a second official record.
event-driven › components › provider-outcome › buildBuy › options › 1 › name: Build on shared parts
event-driven › components › provider-outcome › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: Default, not yet analysed.
event-driven › components › evidence-verification › name: Evidence and verification
event-driven › components › evidence-verification › short: The permanent record of every fact
event-driven › components › evidence-verification › what: The permanent record of every fact the ministry relies on, such as income, rent or family size. Each fact keeps three dates: when it was true, when the ministry recorded it, and, for facts carried over from ICM, when ICM said it.
event-driven › components › evidence-verification › does: Records facts, corrections and changes without ever erasing the old version. It tracks whether each fact has been checked, and announces every change so other parts can act on it.
event-driven › components › evidence-verification › why: A tribunal may ask years later what the ministry knew and when. This record answers that. It also tells a ministry mistake apart from a change in the client's life, which decides whether a client owes money back.
event-driven › components › evidence-verification › buildBuy › label: Build on top of the free event broker
event-driven › components › evidence-verification › buildBuy › summary: The research recommends building the evidence store on the open-source message software. How the ministry records facts, corrections and dates is specific to its needs, and no ordinary database or event store tracks the third date. The independent check noted Cúram also keeps fact history, but as part of one shared case model.
event-driven › components › evidence-verification › buildBuy › options › 1 › name: Evidence store built on Apache Kafka
event-driven › components › evidence-verification › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: Recommended.
event-driven › components › evidence-verification › buildBuy › options › 2 › name: Merative Cúram
event-driven › components › evidence-verification › buildBuy › options › 2 › note: Keeps fact history, but only inside its own case model.
event-driven › components › rules-engine › name: Rules engine
event-driven › components › rules-engine › short: Works out who is eligible, and for what
event-driven › components › rules-engine › what: The part that applies BC's laws and policies to the facts to work out who is eligible and how much they get. Policy staff write the rules; the engine runs them.
event-driven › components › rules-engine › does: Takes the facts and the rules in force on a given date and produces a decision with its reasons. It saves exactly what it used, so any past decision can be re-run and checked.
event-driven › components › rules-engine › why: Rules are BC law written as code, and they change often. Getting them wrong means people are paid wrongly or go without. Letting policy staff test and release rule changes safely saves time and protects clients.
event-driven › components › rules-engine › buildBuy › label: Build the rule-writing tools, on a free open-source engine (ZEN)
event-driven › components › rules-engine › buildBuy › summary: The design has chosen GoRules' free ZEN engine, which runs inside the ministry's own decision service so past decisions can be re-run exactly. The ministry builds the tools to write, test and release rules. GoRules' paid authoring product already covers about two thirds of those tools, so a quote is to be sought for comparison. Oracle Intelligent Advisor and IBM Operational Decision Manager were first ruled out on a wrong fact and could be looked at again.
event-driven › components › rules-engine › buildBuy › options › 1 › name: ZEN engine plus ministry-built tools
event-driven › components › rules-engine › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: Recommended, medium firmness.
event-driven › components › rules-engine › buildBuy › options › 2 › name: GoRules paid authoring product
event-driven › components › rules-engine › buildBuy › options › 2 › note: Quote to be sought for comparison.
event-driven › components › rules-engine › buildBuy › options › 3 › name: Oracle Intelligent Advisor, IBM Operational Decision Manager
event-driven › components › rules-engine › buildBuy › options › 3 › note: Wrongly ruled out at first. Whether to ask them is open again.
event-driven › components › rules-engine › buildBuy › options › 4 › name: InRule
event-driven › components › rules-engine › buildBuy › options › 4 › note: Runs only as a separate network service, so it cannot re-run past decisions the way the design requires.
event-driven › components › rules-engine › watch › text: Nobody has yet tested whether policy analysts can write and release a real rate change on their own with these tools. The design calls for two analysts to try it, unassisted.
event-driven › components › orchestration › name: Workflow (orchestration)
event-driven › components › orchestration › short: Moves work between people and systems
event-driven › components › orchestration › what: The part that moves work along: work queues, due dates set by law, supervision and escalation, scheduled reviews, and long jobs like a payment run.
event-driven › components › orchestration › does: Puts tasks in the right queue, tracks deadlines and flags work that is overdue. If a long job fails part way, it picks up where it stopped or undoes the steps already done.
event-driven › components › orchestration › why: Missed deadlines in child protection or on a reconsideration can harm people and break the law. Clear queues and automatic reminders help staff keep on top of their work.
event-driven › components › orchestration › buildBuy › label: Adopt free open-source software (jBPM)
event-driven › components › orchestration › buildBuy › summary: This is a common need with mature products, and every assessment agreed. The strongest option, jBPM, costs nothing to license and can run on the ministry's own servers. Free to license is not free to run: hosting, support and setup need a budget.
event-driven › components › orchestration › buildBuy › options › 1 › name: jBPM
event-driven › components › orchestration › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: Recommended. Must be tested on undoing steps cleanly.
event-driven › components › orchestration › buildBuy › options › 2 › name: Orkes Conductor
event-driven › components › orchestration › buildBuy › options › 2 › note: Commercial. Can keep a current copy of data on ministry servers.
event-driven › components › orchestration › buildBuy › options › 3 › name: Camunda and Flowable cloud services
event-driven › components › orchestration › buildBuy › options › 3 › note: Not for this core part. Cannot show a ministry-held copy of data.
event-driven › components › orchestration › buildBuy › options › 4 › name: Temporal Cloud
event-driven › components › orchestration › buildBuy › options › 4 › note: Copies only finished work, not work in progress.
event-driven › components › intelligence › name: Intelligence
event-driven › components › intelligence › short: Learning from the data
event-driven › components › intelligence › what: Tools for studying the ministry's data as a whole: spotting trends, planning services and, in future, using machine learning on data with personal details removed.
event-driven › components › intelligence › does: Lets analysts ask questions of the data without making new copies of it. Any work in the public cloud uses only data stripped of personal details.
event-driven › components › intelligence › why: Today data is copied again and again for reports, and each copy is a privacy risk. Asking questions of one well-protected store means better planning with less exposure.
event-driven › components › intelligence › buildBuy › label: Not yet analysed (default: free open-source tools)
event-driven › components › intelligence › buildBuy › summary: The build-vs-buy research did not cover this part. The design names free open-source tools, such as Apache Spark, working over one protected data store on the ministry's own servers. Treat that as the default until it is analysed.
event-driven › components › intelligence › buildBuy › options › 1 › name: Apache Spark and related open-source tools
event-driven › components › intelligence › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: Named in the design. Not yet analysed.
event-driven › components › event-broker › name: Event broker
event-driven › components › event-broker › short: Carries news of every change
event-driven › components › event-broker › what: The message line that links all the parts. An event is a short message that says something happened, like "income reported" or "payment approved". The broker delivers each event to every part that needs to know.
event-driven › components › event-broker › does: Carries every fact and decision between the parts, and checks each message has the agreed shape. It keeps messages in order so a part that was offline can catch up.
event-driven › components › event-broker › why: Because parts only talk through events, any part can be swapped out without rewiring the others. This is what lets ICM be replaced a piece at a time.
event-driven › components › event-broker › buildBuy › label: Adopt free open-source software (Apache Kafka with Strimzi)
event-driven › components › event-broker › buildBuy › summary: The messaging layer is standard, widely used and free to license. The research recommends Apache Kafka, run on the Province's private cloud with the Strimzi tool, and an open-source register of message formats. Some commercial versions carry licence terms that limit how they can be used, so they are not recommended.
event-driven › components › event-broker › buildBuy › options › 1 › name: Apache Kafka with Strimzi
event-driven › components › event-broker › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: Recommended.
event-driven › components › event-broker › buildBuy › options › 2 › name: Apicurio Registry or Karapace
event-driven › components › event-broker › buildBuy › options › 2 › note: Register of agreed message formats.
event-driven › components › event-broker › buildBuy › options › 3 › name: Confluent
event-driven › components › event-broker › buildBuy › options › 3 › note: Not recommended. Licence terms restrict use.
event-driven › components › event-broker › buildBuy › options › 4 › name: Redpanda
event-driven › components › event-broker › buildBuy › options › 4 › note: Not recommended. Useful features are behind a paid licence.
event-driven › components › event-broker › watch › text: Kafka is not yet on the provincial platform's supported list, so the support arrangement must be confirmed in writing first. Teams must also hold the line on the agreed message formats, or the parts will tangle again.
event-driven › components › client-identity › name: Client identity service
event-driven › components › client-identity › short: Proving who a client is
event-driven › components › client-identity › what: The provincial BC Services Card service, which proves a person is who they say they are when they sign in online.
event-driven › components › client-identity › does: Confirms a client's identity at a high level of trust. The ministry keeps a reference to the result, not a copy of the person's details.
event-driven › components › client-identity › why: Clients use the same card they use for other provincial services. The ministry does not have to build or guard its own identity checks, and it holds less personal data.
event-driven › components › client-identity › buildBuy › label: Existing: BC Services Card
event-driven › components › client-identity › buildBuy › summary: The design treats identity as a common service and says reusing the provincial service is not a close call. The BC Services Card service is in production and is reached through the Province's single sign-on.

event-driven › components › client-identity › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: In production.
event-driven › components › notifications › name: Notifications
event-driven › components › notifications › short: Emails and text messages
event-driven › components › notifications › what: The service that sends emails and text messages to clients and partners.
event-driven › components › notifications › does: Sends reminders, alerts and notice that a new letter is ready, and reports back whether each message was delivered.
event-driven › components › notifications › why: A timely reminder can stop a missed deadline or a cut-off payment. Reusing a government service saves building and running one.
event-driven › components › notifications › buildBuy › label: Existing: provincial notification service, with a fallback
event-driven › components › notifications › buildBuy › summary: The design reuses the Province's notification service, which is still being developed. Because it may not be ready in time, it names fallbacks: the federal GC Notify service or the Province's Common Hosted Email Service.
event-driven › components › notifications › buildBuy › options › 1 › name: Provincial notification service
event-driven › components › notifications › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: In development. Readiness date to confirm.

event-driven › components › notifications › buildBuy › options › 3 › name: GC Notify
event-driven › components › notifications › buildBuy › options › 3 › note: Federal service. Fallback, sends up to Protected A messages.
event-driven › components › documents › name: Documents
event-driven › components › documents › short: Letters, notices and signatures
event-driven › components › documents › what: The tools that build letters and notices from each decision, store documents, and collect electronic signatures.
event-driven › components › documents › does: Fills a notice template with the decision, its reasons and the client's appeal rights. It stores documents and links each one to the fact it supports.
event-driven › components › documents › why: A notice must always match its decision and state the right appeal period. Getting this right protects clients' rights and the ministry at a tribunal.
event-driven › components › documents › buildBuy › label: Buy or adopt several tools; build the link to each decision
event-driven › components › documents › buildBuy › summary: Producing, storing and signing documents are common needs with many low-cost tools. The research recommends using provincial services where they fit, buying or adopting the rest, and building only the link that ties each notice to its decision. Expect several tools, not one. A request for information on electronic signatures was proposed.

event-driven › components › documents › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: Provincial service for building documents from templates.

event-driven › components › documents › buildBuy › options › 4 › name: Documenso, DocuSeal
event-driven › components › documents › buildBuy › options › 4 › note: Free electronic signature options.
event-driven › components › documents › watch › text: Per-user pricing for electronic signatures could become large if every staff account needs a licence.
event-driven › components › chat-bots › name: Chat bots
event-driven › components › chat-bots › short: Automatic answers to common questions
event-driven › components › chat-bots › what: Online helpers that answer common questions by chat, any time of day.
event-driven › components › chat-bots › does: Answers questions like when the next payment is due or what documents to bring, and passes harder questions to a person.
event-driven › components › chat-bots › why: Quick answers to simple questions can cut phone wait times and free staff for clients who need more help.
event-driven › components › chat-bots › buildBuy › label: Not yet analysed (default: buy or reuse)
event-driven › components › chat-bots › buildBuy › summary: No build-vs-buy analysis has been done for chat bots yet. As a common tool, the design's rule points to buying or reusing one rather than building it, and it must never make decisions about eligibility.

event-driven › components › printing › name: Printing
event-driven › components › printing › short: Paper letters and cheques
event-driven › components › printing › what: The Province's own print-and-mail service, which prints and posts letters and cheques.
event-driven › components › printing › does: Receives letters and cheques in batches, prints them and mails them, and reports back when they were sent.
event-driven › components › printing › why: Many clients rely on paper. When a client prefers paper, every decision notice goes out on paper by default, with the same deadlines as online.

event-driven › components › document-scanning › what: Tools that scan paper documents, sort them, and read key details from them.
event-driven › components › document-scanning › does: Takes in documents from mail, fax, email, uploads and offices. It records the date each arrived, because legal deadlines run from that date.
event-driven › components › document-scanning › why: Lost or slow paperwork delays decisions. Values read by a machine are treated as unconfirmed until checked, so a scanning error cannot silently change a client's benefit.

event-driven › components › payment-processing › name: Payment processing
event-driven › components › payment-processing › short: Sends money by deposit and cheque
event-driven › components › payment-processing › what: The single controlled path every payment leaves by: the monthly and off-cycle payment runs, direct deposit and cheques.
event-driven › components › payment-processing › does: Takes approved payment instructions and sends the money. It handles stop payments, reissues, returned payments and month-end cutoffs, and makes sure nothing is paid twice.
event-driven › components › payment-processing › why: A system that decides correctly but does not pay has failed completely. Clients depend on these payments for basic needs, so this part comes first if a supplier ever cuts off access.
event-driven › components › payment-processing › buildBuy › label: Build one payment service (proposed); reuse provincial services

The highest-scoring products held payments, ledgers and debts together, which the design does not allow, and no hosted product showed it keeps data in Canada with a ministry-held copy. Card payments go through the Province's approved payment path, and the corporate financial system remains the official book. This direction is in a decision record not yet accepted.

event-driven › components › payment-processing › buildBuy › options › 4 › note: Not shortlisted. None showed Canadian data or a ministry-held copy.
event-driven › components › payment-processing › watch › text: Provincial policy says payments are made by the Ministry of Finance unless approved otherwise. Whether the ministry sends a file to the bank at all, and in what format, is not yet known.

event-driven › components › policy-governance › what: Rules about who may see or change which records, written down as tested files rather than settings scattered across the system.
event-driven › components › policy-governance › does: Checks every request against the access rules and records who looked at what, for what purpose, and under what law.
event-driven › components › policy-governance › why: An audit found over a third of ICM's 9,400 users had access outside the approved model. Written, tested rules make it clear who can see a child protection file, and why.

event-driven › components › data-gateway › name: Data integration gateway
event-driven › components › data-gateway › short: Sharing data with other organisations
event-driven › components › data-gateway › what: The approved route for sharing information with other ministries and organisations, through the Province's Secure Data Exchange.
event-driven › components › data-gateway › does: Checks that each exchange is allowed under a recorded agreement and law, sends it securely, and keeps proof of what was shared.
event-driven › components › data-gateway › why: Clients' information must only go where the law allows. Keeping proof of every exchange protects clients and lets the ministry answer access-to-information requests.
