event-driven › components › icm-api › name: ICM API
event-driven › components › icm-api › short: Temporary bridge to the old system
event-driven › components › icm-api › what: A temporary bridge into ICM, so new parts and ICM can work side by side while ICM is replaced piece by piece.
event-driven › components › icm-api › does: Translates requests between the new system's language and ICM's. It sends changes made in ICM out as events, and writes back to ICM where needed.
event-driven › components › icm-api › why: It avoids a risky single switch-over day. Its team's job is to shrink it until it can be turned off, so ICM is truly retired and its costs end.
event-driven › components › icm-api › buildBuy › label: Build, then remove
event-driven › components › icm-api › buildBuy › summary: Nothing on the market is shaped like a bridge to one specific old system that is meant to be thrown away. The ministry builds it, and its team is set up to take it apart. It also needs changes inside ICM itself, made by whoever holds ICM's configuration.
event-driven › components › icm-api › buildBuy › options › 1 › name: Ministry-built bridge
event-driven › components › icm-api › buildBuy › options › 1 › note: Temporary by design.
event-driven › components › icm-api › watch › text: A partial API over ICM is already in use. If it exposes ICM's own codes and record numbers, the people using it are tied to ICM. A decision is needed before more users depend on it.

=== src/lib/content/home.yaml
home › compare › heading: The options side by side
home › compare › rows › 1 › question: Who controls when it changes?
home › compare › rows › 1 › s: SaaS Provider. SaaS providers set the update cadence, and CSBC cannot pause them.
home › compare › rows › 1 › h: SaaS Provider for case work and rules. CSBC for the payment run.
home › compare › rows › 1 › e: CSBC. It runs the parts on its own servers and sets its own timing.
home › compare › rows › 2 › question: What happens if the supplier cuts us off?
home › compare › rows › 2 › s: A copy of records can be kept. Payments fall back to a manual procedure.
home › compare › rows › 2 › h: A ministry copy keeps intake, case viewing and payment records - processing proceeds as normal.
home › compare › rows › 2 › e: Data stays on ministry servers. Strategic component selection reduces reliance on one supplier.
home › compare › rows › 3 › question: Where does the money run?
home › compare › rows › 3 › s: Using the CRM account ledger, pushed to a monthly batch EFT process, print cheques require custom solution.
home › compare › rows › 3 › h: On the ministry's own servers, with the ministry's own ledger, EFTs can use existing components, print cheques can proceed as is.
home › compare › rows › 3 › e: In payment and finance parts built for the ministry, on its own servers. Payment methods and processes can be fine-tuned.
home › compare › rows › 4 › question: How much custom work?
home › compare › rows › 4 › s: A lot. Only about 1/4 of functionality comes "out of the box", half can be built using the platform's tools, with the remainder being custom extensions to the platform.
home › compare › rows › 4 › h: By moving some functionality off to separate component, more functionality is available by default, that is partially offset by integration work. Custom work remains relatively constant.
home › compare › rows › 4 › e: Maximal use of acquired or adopted components; custom development only where business needs are unique.
home › compare › rows › 5 › question: What are the yearly licence costs?
home › compare › rows › 5 › s: About $44M to $80M a year at list price, before any discount.
home › compare › rows › 5 › h: About $44M to $80M a year at list price, before any discount.
home › compare › rows › 5 › e: Variable based on components purchased vs. developed.
home › compare › rows › 6 › question: Do we lose anything by migrating?
home › compare › rows › 6 › s: Yes. The ministry loses its change freeze around the monthly cheque run.
home › compare › rows › 6 › h: Less so. The payment run keeps its freeze; work on the CRM platform does not.
home › compare › rows › 6 › e: This can be chosen rather than determined by vendor choices.
home › compare › rows › 7 › question: When could people use something new (assuming a product team of approx. 12)?
home › compare › rows › 7 › s: With a product team of 12, about 13 months after licenses are acquired.
home › compare › rows › 7 › h: 13 months after license procurement, though some non-user-facing components can be be built before licensing.
home › compare › rows › 7 › e: Depending on sequencing choices, as early as month three - but most likely month nine.
home › cta › heading: Start with an option
home › cta › text: Pick an option to see its diagram and what it would mean for staff, clients and money.
home › hero › title: Three ways to replace ICM
home › hero › lede: ICM powers the social sector. This site shows three ways it could be replaced.
home › howToRead › heading: How to read the diagrams
home › howToRead › steps › 1: Each option has a diagram. Boxes are grouped by who runs them, such as the SaaS provider or the ministry.
home › howToRead › steps › 2: Click or tap any box to learn what it is, what it does and why it matters.
home › howToRead › steps › 3: Look for the coloured notes. They show where an option falls short or fixes a problem.
home › optionsIntro › heading: The three options
home › optionsIntro › text: SaaS S puts everything on a SaaS CRM and runs it the way ICM runs today. SaaS H has the SaaS product used for case work and rules, and keeps money, evidence and records on the ministry's own servers. Event-driven has the ministry build in parts buy or adopt common components, and link them through an event stream updated when something happens, such as a payment being issued.
home › why › heading: Why ICM needs replacing
home › why › paragraphs › 1: ICM works...except when it doesn't. It takes a lot of effort to keep it working. Workers must contend with an arcane and complex system that makes even simple things tediously complex and slow.
home › why › paragraphs › 2: It is not just slow or clunky, ICM is missing core capabilities such as the ability to manage monthly payments. It has failed to keep pace with the changes needed by business - leading to a sprawling mess of hacks, workarounds and bolt-ons.
home › why › paragraphs › 3: ICM costs more and more each year, but the value it provides has been shrinking, and it never delivered on its promises.

=== src/lib/content/problems.yaml
problems › intro: ICM-Siebel has carried social sector business processes for many years. Thousands of front-line staff make it work daily, often by working around it. This page outlines a handful of problems people run into and have been the subject of voluble and long-running complaints. It is important to draw the right lessons from each problem by identifying the root cause - which tells us what a replacement has to do differently.
problems › problems › 1 › title: Clunky, Slow, Obtuse UX
problems › problems › 1 › who: Everyone who uses ICM
problems › problems › 1 › see: Simple tasks are convoluted. Everything is complicated. Spinny wheel forever. Six weeks of training to just use a case management system.
problems › problems › 1 › apparent: The system is old. Bad engineering has bogged it down. It's too bloated. Nobody listens to users.
problems › problems › 1 › real: The way Siebel is designed makes feature development indirect and very rigidly constrained. Because Siebel has one UX for everyone, the UI remains generic, rather than ergonomic. The data model in Siebel makes it difficult to create fast behaviour, and easy to make very slow features.
problems › problems › 1 › example: Displaying a single PDF form can take a dozen clicks, and tens of minutes to render. Some queries can bog the system down so badly it crashes. The UI has not been updated since 2011.
problems › problems › 2 › title: Even small changes are expensive, slow and risky
problems › problems › 2 › who: EAWs, managers
problems › problems › 2 › see: Release management is an Apollo launch mission. The live defect count will never reach zero. Each problem gets worse, problems get more frequent, and enhancement requests get sliced thinner and thinner. The cost of the system climbs steadily despite producing the same or less value.
problems › problems › 2 › apparent: Sloppy and hasty work has accumulated technical debt that never got paid down.
problems › problems › 2 › real: Case-file centricity means every system component depends on a single core entity. Limitations of the model and the way features can be developed require hacky work arounds as the only viable solution. The core system mismatches the business domain, resulting in bolted-on features which are difficult to test.
problems › problems › 2 › example: Invalid EFT information can go unnoticed until after cheque issue. Social insurance numbers can be arbitrary strings. A defect in one small component can cascade to a full system failure, resulting in roll-backs, emergency fixes and heroics. Defects can go undetected or unremedied for months or years - and are almost always discovered first by end users.
problems › problems › 3 › title: Core features are after thoughts.
problems › problems › 3 › who: Policy, EAWs, operations teams
problems › problems › 3 › see: Core business activities involved heavy customizations, hacks and bolt-on components to make possible.
problems › problems › 3 › apparent: COTS + Customization is a common anti-pattern.
problems › problems › 3 › real: System was selected for fit on only a single dimension. Siebel, a monolithic application, was treated like a platform. Many features were anticipated to be native, never materialized.
problems › problems › 3 › example: Complex financial processing remains locked with MIS because no equivalent capability is possible within Siebel. Cheque issue, the most important activity in the social sector, and Siebel can't deliver it.
problems › problems › 4 › title: Extension is infeasible
problems › problems › 4 › who: EAWs, partner programs, clients
problems › problems › 4 › see: ICM's API requires a "Trusted Systems" model that doesn't scale and conflicts with government strategy.
problems › problems › 4 › apparent: The system has been too heavily customized to use an API.
problems › problems › 4 › real: The API circumvents all authorization access requiring downstream applications to implement all security measures. The data schema is unintelligible without the application layer to link things together.
problems › problems › 4 › example: CFD Mobility project must maintain a large middleware stack to compensate for the lack of a security service. Request payloads require processing overhead of Siebel even for simple queries.
problems › problems › 5 › title: Auditing and reviews rely on poor security practice
problems › problems › 5 › who: Security and privacy staff, Managers, Tribunals and Auditors.
problems › problems › 5 › see: System logs are the primary mechanism for auditing system behaviour, including user actions and evaluations. The system itself has no concept of change over time, and so tracking data changes is a special feature for each instance. System logs capture highly sensitive information in plain text in a consolidated, easily downloaded format. Auditing and incident response is a sleuthing exercise rather than a simple query.
problems › problems › 5 › apparent: It has not been prioritized as a target for development.
problems › problems › 5 › real: ICM lacks an alternative structure to capture bitemporal information - it is completely out of band. Change events are captured implicitly by the database and are not themselves system data. The sensitivity of the log contents and lack of protections eliminate most log processing tools from consideration.
problems › problems › 5 › example: An information incident requires manual recovery and are typically only discovered well after the fact. Tribunals rely on incomplete information when making determinations - because full details are not captured.

=== src/lib/content/timeline.yaml
timeline › plans › s › summary: A planning sketch, not a commitment. Everything moves onto the CRM platform and runs the way ICM (today's case system) runs now. The first 7 months go to design work while CRM and integration platform licences are bought, because almost nothing can be built without them. After that, a release goes out every 3 months, one program at a time, from the smallest programs to child protection.
timeline › plans › s › realism: The research puts the CRM build at 19,385 person-days, its likely figure. This team can do about 2,640 person-days a year. 19,385 divided by 2,640 is 7.3 years of build. Once the first release is live, the team must also retest the system before each of the CRM provider's three upgrades a year, about 135 person-days a year. That adds about 4 months. With the 7-month wait for licences, the plan runs about 100 months, a little over 8 years. With 10 people it is closer to 10 years; with 14, about 7. The research's own range, 12,475 to 29,940 person-days, means anywhere from about 4 to 14 years of build. The estimate also leaves out project management, training, running ICM and CRM side by side, and contingency, so the real time will be longer. Two teams of this size could bring the whole plan down to roughly 4 and a half years, if the work splits cleanly between them. It rarely splits perfectly.
timeline › plans › s › assumptions › 1: Procurement lead times are planning assumptions, not figures from the research. We assume 4 to 9 months for a large competitive purchase, and 2 to 4 months when an existing agreement or standing offer can be used.
timeline › plans › s › assumptions › 2: We count the whole team of 12 as delivery capacity: 12 people times 220 working days is 2,640 person-days a year. That is generous, because the director and product manager will not build software.
timeline › plans › s › assumptions › 3: Effort comes from the SaaS CRM research (19,385 person-days likely). It assumes a mixed team of CRM specialists, integration and data engineers, and testers. This team has no dedicated testers or integration engineers, so developers cover that work or the team hires for it.
timeline › plans › s › assumptions › 4: The 7 months before building starts are spent on discovery, service design and a prototype on the CRM provider's free trial systems, using made-up data only. That design work is not counted in the build estimate.
timeline › plans › s › assumptions › 5: The ministry already runs the CRM platform for its contract management system and some portals. Buying through that relationship might shorten the 7-month licence wait. Whether the new system shares that CRM setup or has its own is still an open question.
timeline › plans › s › assumptions › 6: Licences for about 9,400 staff are listed at roughly 31 to 56 million US dollars a year before discounts. We assume they can be bought in steps as each program moves. The CRM provider has not been asked.
timeline › plans › s › assumptions › 7: The order of programs follows the target architecture's rule: smallest set of rules and lowest harm first, employment assistance late, child protection last.
timeline › plans › s › assumptions › 8: Before any program's decisions go live, the CRM provider's answers are checked against ICM's for three monthly cycles, as the research assumes.
timeline › plans › s › assumptions › 9: Payment work assumes the Comptroller General's office accepts a new ministry payment system. Provincial policy requires that, and nobody has asked yet. The bank's file format is also not confirmed.
timeline › plans › s › assumptions › 10: The CRM provider's limit on how often its rules engine can be called each month is not confirmed. A low limit could slow the side-by-side checks.
timeline › plans › s › assumptions › 11: Child protection estimates have not had a second reader, so they may grow.
timeline › plans › s › assumptions › 12: Moving onto the CRM platform needs written exceptions to four requirements, including keeping payments going if the supplier cuts off access. This plan assumes those are approved before building starts.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 1 › name: Discovery and design while licences are bought
timeline › plans › s › phases › 1 › goal: Learn how the work is done today and design the first releases while procurement runs.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 2 › name: Set up the CRM platform and the link to ICM
timeline › plans › s › phases › 2 › goal: Set up the CRM platform, its security and access rules, and the integration platform link that reads from and writes to ICM.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 3 › name: First release: a better worker view
timeline › plans › s › phases › 3 › goal: Give workers a fast client search and a one-page case summary, read from ICM, without changing how cases are decided.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 3 › releases › 1 › name: Pilot in one office
timeline › plans › s › phases › 3 › releases › 1 › who: Workers in one office
timeline › plans › s › phases › 3 › releases › 1 › what: Search for a client and see a one-page summary of their cases. ICM stays the official record, so nothing done here can damage it.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 3 › releases › 2 › name: All offices
timeline › plans › s › phases › 3 › releases › 2 › who: Workers in every office
timeline › plans › s › phases › 3 › releases › 2 › what: The same search and summary, with fixes from the pilot.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › name: Two smaller programs first
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › goal: Move child care subsidy and employment services first, because their rules are the smallest and a mistake does the least harm.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 1 › name: Online application, one region
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 1 › who: New child care subsidy applicants in one region, and their workers
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 1 › what: Apply online and upload documents. Each application is copied into ICM, so nothing is lost.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 2 › name: Decisions and letters
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 2 › who: Child care subsidy workers
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 2 › what: Eligibility is worked out by rules kept in the CRM platform, and the letter is made from the decision.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 3 › name: Existing cases move
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 3 › who: All child care subsidy clients and workers
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 3 › what: Open cases move from ICM in groups. A group can be moved back if something goes wrong.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 4 › name: Employment services referrals and plans
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 4 › who: Employment services workers and service providers
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 4 › what: Referrals and plans are made in the CRM platform. Providers use a partner website.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 5 › name: Employment services cases move
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 5 › who: All employment services clients and workers
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 5 › what: Open cases move from ICM in groups.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 6 › name: Reviews and appeals
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 6 › who: Clients asking for a review, and the staff who handle it
timeline › plans › s › phases › 4 › releases › 6 › what: Requests to review a decision, and their legal deadlines, are handled in the CRM platform for both programs.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 5 › name: Payments and overpayments
timeline › plans › s › phases › 5 › goal: Pay clients of the moved programs from the CRM platform, with files sent to the bank, BC Mail Plus and the government's accounting system through the integration platform.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 5 › releases › 1 › name: Side-by-side payment run
timeline › plans › s › phases › 5 › releases › 1 › who: Finance staff
timeline › plans › s › phases › 5 › releases › 1 › what: The CRM platform works out each payment while the old system still pays. Staff compare the two each month. No money moves from the CRM platform yet.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 5 › releases › 2 › name: First live payment run
timeline › plans › s › phases › 5 › releases › 2 › who: Child care subsidy and employment services clients
timeline › plans › s › phases › 5 › releases › 2 › what: Payments for these two programs are issued from the CRM platform.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 5 › releases › 3 › name: Overpayments and debts
timeline › plans › s › phases › 5 › releases › 3 › who: Finance and recovery staff
timeline › plans › s › phases › 5 › releases › 3 › what: Overpayments and repayments are recorded in the CRM platform. They are no longer printed, scanned and typed into another system.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › name: Disability assistance and employment assistance
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › goal: Move the two largest programs together, late on purpose, because a wrong answer here can mean someone cannot buy food this month.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 1 › name: Online monthly report, one region
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 1 › who: Employment assistance clients in one region
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 1 › what: Send the monthly report online. ICM still makes the decision.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 2 › name: Disability applications online
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 2 › who: People applying for disability assistance, and people helping them
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 2 › what: Apply online and see where the application is.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 3 › name: Side-by-side decisions
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 3 › who: Program staff
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 3 › what: The CRM platform works out entitlement for real cases next to ICM for three monthly cycles. Every difference is explained before anyone relies on the new answer.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 4 › name: First region moves
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 4 › who: Clients and workers in one region
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 4 › what: Cases, decisions, letters and payments for both programs move to the CRM platform together, because the disability decision sets the rate employment assistance pays.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 5 › name: Two more regions
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 5 › who: Clients and workers in two more regions
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 5 › what: The same move, with fixes from the first region.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 6 › name: Half the province
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 6 › who: Clients and workers in about half the province
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 6 › what: More regions move in groups.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 7 › name: Rest of the province
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 7 › who: All remaining clients and workers in both programs
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 7 › what: The rest of the caseload moves. ICM no longer handles these programs.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 8 › name: Old screens switched off
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 8 › who: Workers in both programs
timeline › plans › s › phases › 6 › releases › 8 › what: ICM screens and links for these programs are turned off.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › name: Child protection
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › goal: Move child protection last, with its own design work, because it has the least structured practice, the strictest privacy needs and court-ordered records.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 1 › name: Caregivers and providers
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 1 › who: Foster caregivers, service providers and the workers who support them
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 1 › what: Caregiver and provider records and licensing move to the CRM platform, with a partner website.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 2 › name: Family plans and agreements
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 2 › who: Child protection workers
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 2 › what: Care plans and agreements with families are made and tracked in the CRM platform.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 3 › name: Court documents
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 3 › who: Child protection workers who go to court
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 3 › what: Court proceedings and orders are tracked in the CRM platform. About 150 forms and letters are made there.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 4 › name: Visits on mobile
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 4 › who: Workers visiting families in remote areas
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 4 › what: Record visits on a phone or tablet, even with no signal.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 5 › name: Reports of concern
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 5 › who: The 24/7 reporting line and intake workers
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 5 › what: Calls about a child's safety go straight into the case. A backup way to record reports is used during the CRM provider's maintenance windows.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 6 › name: Investigations
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 6 › who: Child protection workers
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 6 › what: Investigations and safety assessments are done in the CRM platform.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 7 › name: Adoption
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 7 › who: Adoption workers
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 7 › what: Adoption records move to the CRM platform. This is the largest single piece of child protection work.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 8 › name: Remaining cases move
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 8 › who: All child protection workers
timeline › plans › s › phases › 7 › releases › 8 › what: The rest of the open child protection cases move from ICM in groups.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 8 › name: Move the remaining history
timeline › plans › s › phases › 8 › goal: Move closed cases and old records out of ICM with their original dates, and check that every record arrived.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 8 › releases › 1 › name: History check complete
timeline › plans › s › phases › 8 › releases › 1 › who: Records staff and auditors
timeline › plans › s › phases › 8 › releases › 1 › what: Every old record is in the CRM platform or in a checked archive, with its original dates.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 9 › name: Switch off ICM
timeline › plans › s › phases › 9 › goal: Turn off ICM and the Siebel product it runs on, close its links to other systems, and keep a controlled archive.
timeline › plans › s › phases › 9 › releases › 1 › name: ICM switched off
timeline › plans › s › phases › 9 › releases › 1 › who: Everyone
timeline › plans › s › phases › 9 › releases › 1 › what: ICM is turned off. Its licence, support and servers stop costing money.
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 1 › item: CRM licences: the platform, the public sector package, the portal add-on and 24/7 support
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 1 › why: Every CRM screen, form and record runs on these, for about 9,400 staff accounts. Published list prices come to roughly 31 to 56 million US dollars a year before discounts.
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 1 › startBy: Month 0, the day the project starts
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 2 › item: Security, privacy, test data masking and backup add-ons, extra storage and test copies (sandboxes)
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 2 › why: Needed before any real client data goes in. They give encryption, access monitoring, field history, deletion rules, test copies with no personal information, and backups.
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 2 › startBy: Month 0, with the main licences
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 3 › item: The CRM provider's integration platform, run on the ministry's own servers, with its connector for ICM's Siebel product
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 3 › why: The integration platform is the CRM provider's tool for linking systems. It links the CRM platform to ICM while both run, and to the bank, Treasury, BC Mail Plus, the Canada Revenue Agency, courts and others.
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 3 › startBy: Month 0, the day the project starts
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 4 › item: Reporting tools: the CRM provider's analytics tools
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 4 › why: Dashboards for workers and managers, and reports that replace today's data warehouse feeds as each program moves.
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 4 › startBy: By month 8
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 5 › item: Electronic signature service
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 5 › why: The CRM provider does not sell one. The ministry already uses DocuSign with its contract management system, so extending that contract may be quicker.
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 5 › startBy: By month 10
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 6 › item: Virus scanning for uploaded files and a document redaction tool, on the ministry's own servers
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 6 › why: The CRM platform has no built-in scanning of uploads, and no tool for blacking out parts of a record before it is released.
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 6 › startBy: By month 9
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 7 › item: Field service and phone add-ons
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 7 › why: The field service add-on lets child protection workers record visits on a phone or tablet, even offline. Voice connects calls to the 24/7 reporting line to the case.
timeline › plans › s › procurement › 7 › startBy: By month 62
timeline › plans › h › summary: A planning sketch, not a commitment. Case work and rules move onto the CRM platform. Money, evidence, decision records, the event stream and a backup copy of the records stay on the ministry's own servers. The ministry-side parts need no CRM licence, so the team starts building them during the licence wait. Releases then go out every 3 months, one program at a time, as in the all-CRM plan.
timeline › plans › h › realism: The research puts the CRM side at 22,185 person-days, its likely figure. It does not estimate the parts on the ministry's own servers. Other research gives a rough floor for some of them: event stream and evidence store 1,040, payment run 800, ledger 240, and matching accounts with the bank 200. That makes 2,280, and the total at least 24,465. Retesting before the CRM provider's three upgrades a year adds about 1,200 over 9 years. At 2,640 person-days a year, that is 9.7 years of work. About 750 person-days get done during the licence wait, so the plan runs about 120 months, or 10 years. It is still missing the decision record store, the backup copy and its fallback tools, and a backup path for the reporting line, so it will run longer. With 10 people it is about 12 years; with 14, about 8 and a half. Two teams of this size could bring it to roughly 5 and a half years if the work splits cleanly.
timeline › plans › h › assumptions › 1: Procurement lead times are planning assumptions, not figures from the research. We assume 4 to 9 months for a large competitive purchase, and 2 to 4 months when an existing agreement or standing offer can be used.
timeline › plans › h › assumptions › 2: We count the whole team of 12 as delivery capacity: 12 people times 220 working days is 2,640 person-days a year. That is generous, because the director and product manager will not build software.
timeline › plans › h › assumptions › 3: CRM-side effort comes from the SaaS CRM research (22,185 person-days likely). The ministry-side floor comes from rough rules of thumb in the technology and payments research. Those researchers call their figures a floor.
timeline › plans › h › assumptions › 4: In months 2 to 7, part of the team builds the ministry-side parts (about 750 person-days) while others do discovery and service design.
timeline › plans › h › assumptions › 5: The ministry-side parts run on the government's own private cloud. That is an existing service, not a purchase. The event stream software is free, but who supports it on that platform is not confirmed in writing.
timeline › plans › h › assumptions › 6: The ministry already runs the CRM platform for its contract management system and some portals. Buying through that relationship might shorten the 7-month licence wait.
timeline › plans › h › assumptions › 7: Licences for about 9,400 staff are listed at roughly 31 to 56 million US dollars a year before discounts. We assume they can be bought in steps. The CRM provider has not been asked.
timeline › plans › h › assumptions › 8: The backup copy only needs to repeat last month's payments if the CRM provider cuts off access. No business area has asked for more. If more services must keep running, this plan grows.
timeline › plans › h › assumptions › 9: Payment work assumes the Comptroller General's office accepts a new ministry payment system, as provincial policy requires. The bank's file format is also not confirmed.
timeline › plans › h › assumptions › 10: The order of programs follows the target architecture: smallest set of rules and lowest harm first, employment assistance late, child protection last.
timeline › plans › h › assumptions › 11: The CRM provider's monthly limit on rules engine calls is not confirmed. A low limit could slow the side-by-side checks.
timeline › plans › h › assumptions › 12: Child protection estimates have not had a second reader, so they may grow.

timeline › plans › h › phases › 1 › goal: Learn how the work is done today and design the first releases while procurement runs.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 2 › name: Build the ministry-side parts
timeline › plans › h › phases › 2 › goal: Build the parts that live on the ministry's own servers and need no CRM licence: the event stream, the evidence store, the decision record store and the ledger.

timeline › plans › h › phases › 5 › goal: Move child care subsidy and employment services first, with each fact and each decision recorded on the ministry's own servers from day one.

timeline › plans › h › phases › 6 › name: Payments on the ministry's own servers
timeline › plans › h › phases › 6 › goal: Run payments, the ledger and daily account matching on the ministry's own servers, on the ministry's own release calendar.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 6 › releases › 1 › name: Side-by-side payment run
timeline › plans › h › phases › 6 › releases › 1 › who: Finance staff
timeline › plans › h › phases › 6 › releases › 1 › what: The new payment run works out each payment while the old system still pays. Staff compare the two each month. No money moves yet.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 6 › releases › 2 › name: First live payment run
timeline › plans › h › phases › 6 › releases › 2 › who: Child care subsidy and employment services clients
timeline › plans › h › phases › 6 › releases › 2 › what: Payments for these two programs come from the ministry's own payment run. CRM upgrades cannot interrupt it.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 6 › releases › 3 › name: Daily matching
timeline › plans › h › phases › 6 › releases › 3 › who: Finance staff
timeline › plans › h › phases › 6 › releases › 3 › what: Every day, the ministry's ledger is matched against the bank and the government's accounts. Each mismatch is tracked until it is cleared.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 6 › releases › 4 › name: Cut-off rehearsal
timeline › plans › h › phases › 6 › releases › 4 › who: Finance and operations staff
timeline › plans › h › phases › 6 › releases › 4 › what: With the CRM platform switched off in a test, the backup copy repeats last month's payments through the same controls.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 6 › releases › 5 › name: Overpayments and debts
timeline › plans › h › phases › 6 › releases › 5 › who: Finance and recovery staff

timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › name: Disability assistance and employment assistance
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › goal: Move the two largest programs together, late on purpose, because a wrong answer here can mean someone cannot buy food this month.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 1 › name: Online monthly report, one region
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 1 › who: Employment assistance clients in one region
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 1 › what: Send the monthly report online. ICM still makes the decision.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 2 › name: Disability applications online
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 2 › who: People applying for disability assistance, and people helping them
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 2 › what: Apply online and see where the application is.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 3 › name: Side-by-side decisions
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 3 › who: Program staff
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 3 › what: The CRM platform works out entitlement for real cases next to ICM for three monthly cycles. Every difference is explained before anyone relies on the new answer.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 4 › name: First region moves
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 4 › who: Clients and workers in one region
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 4 › what: Cases and decisions move to the CRM platform and payments move to the ministry's payment run, for both programs together.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 5 › name: Two more regions
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 5 › who: Clients and workers in two more regions
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 5 › what: The same move, with fixes from the first region.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 6 › name: Half the province
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 6 › who: Clients and workers in about half the province

timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 7 › name: More regions
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 7 › who: Clients and workers in further regions
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 7 › what: More regions move in groups.

timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 8 › who: All remaining clients and workers in both programs
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 8 › what: The rest of the caseload moves. ICM no longer handles these programs.

timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 9 › who: Workers in both programs
timeline › plans › h › phases › 7 › releases › 9 › what: ICM screens and links for these programs are turned off.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › name: Child protection
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › goal: Move child protection last, with its own design work, because it has the least structured practice, the strictest privacy needs and court-ordered records.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 1 › name: Caregivers and providers
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 1 › who: Foster caregivers, service providers and the workers who support them
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 1 › what: Caregiver and provider records and licensing move to the CRM platform, with a partner website.

timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 2 › who: Child protection workers
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 2 › what: Care plans and agreements with families are made and tracked in the CRM platform.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 3 › name: Court documents
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 3 › who: Child protection workers who go to court
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 3 › what: Court proceedings and orders are tracked in the CRM platform. About 150 forms and letters are made there.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 4 › name: Visits on mobile
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 4 › who: Workers visiting families in remote areas
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 4 › what: Record visits on a phone or tablet, even with no signal.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 5 › name: Reports of concern
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 5 › who: The 24/7 reporting line and intake workers
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 5 › what: Calls about a child's safety go straight into the case. A backup intake path on the ministry's servers works when the CRM platform is down.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 6 › name: Investigations
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 6 › who: Child protection workers
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 6 › what: Investigations and safety assessments are done in the CRM platform.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 7 › name: Adoption
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 7 › who: Adoption workers
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 7 › what: Adoption records move to the CRM platform. This is the largest single piece of child protection work.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 8 › name: Remaining cases move
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 8 › who: All child protection workers
timeline › plans › h › phases › 8 › releases › 8 › what: The rest of the open child protection cases move from ICM in groups.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 9 › name: Move the remaining history
timeline › plans › h › phases › 9 › goal: Move closed cases and old records out of ICM with their original dates, and check that every record arrived.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 9 › releases › 1 › name: History check complete
timeline › plans › h › phases › 9 › releases › 1 › who: Records staff and auditors
timeline › plans › h › phases › 9 › releases › 1 › what: Every old record is in the new system or in a checked archive, with its original dates.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 10 › name: Switch off ICM
timeline › plans › h › phases › 10 › goal: Turn off ICM and the Siebel product it runs on, close its links to other systems, and keep a controlled archive.
timeline › plans › h › phases › 10 › releases › 1 › name: ICM switched off
timeline › plans › h › phases › 10 › releases › 1 › who: Everyone
timeline › plans › h › phases › 10 › releases › 1 › what: ICM is turned off. Its licence, support and servers stop costing money.
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 1 › item: CRM licences: the platform, the public sector package, the portal add-on and 24/7 support
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 1 › why: Every CRM screen, form and record runs on these, for about 9,400 staff accounts. Published list prices come to roughly 31 to 56 million US dollars a year before discounts.
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 1 › startBy: Month 0, the day the project starts
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 2 › item: Security, privacy, test data masking and backup add-ons, extra storage and test copies (sandboxes)
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 2 › why: Needed before any real client data goes in. They give encryption, access monitoring, field history, deletion rules, test copies with no personal information, and backups.
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 2 › startBy: Month 0, with the main licences
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 3 › item: The CRM provider's integration platform, run on the ministry's own servers, with its connector for ICM's Siebel product
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 3 › why: The integration platform is the CRM provider's tool for linking systems. Here it links the CRM platform to ICM, to the ministry-side parts, and to the bank, Treasury, courts and others.
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 3 › startBy: Month 0, the day the project starts
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 4 › item: Support contract for the event stream software (Apache Kafka), only if the government's private cloud team cannot support it
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 4 › why: The event stream carries every fact and decision between the CRM platform and the ministry-side parts. The software is free, but someone must be on call when it breaks.
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 4 › startBy: Month 1
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 5 › item: Reporting tools: the CRM provider's analytics tools
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 5 › why: Dashboards for workers and managers, and reports that replace today's data warehouse feeds as each program moves.
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 5 › startBy: By month 9
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 6 › item: Electronic signature service
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 6 › why: The CRM provider does not sell one. The ministry already uses DocuSign with its contract management system, so extending that contract may be quicker.
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 6 › startBy: By month 11
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 7 › item: Virus scanning for uploaded files and a document redaction tool, on the ministry's own servers
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 7 › why: The CRM platform has no built-in scanning of uploads, and no tool for blacking out parts of a record before it is released.
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 7 › startBy: By month 10
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 8 › item: Account matching (reconciliation) product, only if the ministry decides to buy rather than build
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 8 › why: Matches the ministry's ledger with the bank and the government's accounts every day. It is the one payments part where buying is plausible. A request for information is drafted but not sent.
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 8 › startBy: By month 28
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 9 › item: Field service and phone add-ons
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 9 › why: The field service add-on lets child protection workers record visits on a phone or tablet, even offline. Voice connects calls to the 24/7 reporting line to the case.
timeline › plans › h › procurement › 9 › startBy: By month 74
timeline › plans › e › summary: A planning sketch, not a commitment. The ministry builds its own target design in parts, using free open-source software and services the government already runs, and buys only a few common tools. With no big licence to wait for, a first worker release can come in month 9. Releases then go out every 3 months, and each part of ICM is switched off as its replacement lands.
timeline › plans › e › realism: No one has made a bottom-up estimate for this option, so we built one. The technology and payments research gives a floor for the ten main parts: 13,040 person-days. That floor leaves out child protection, moving data and links to other organizations. For those we borrowed the SaaS CRM research's figures as stand-ins: child protection 6,495, moving data 1,330, links 1,140 and running beside ICM 930. The total is 22,935. At 2,640 person-days a year that is 8.7 years. Starting after 2 months of discovery, the plan runs about 106 months. With 10 people it is about 10 and a half years; with 14, about 7 and a half. This is the least certain of the three figures. The target architecture's own costing for the full design is 142 to 249 million dollars over 9 to 13 years, with 55 to 110 people. At its own rates that is roughly 350 to 960 person-years of work, because it also counts project management, training, running two systems side by side and contingency. At 12 people that would take 30 to 80 years. So one team this size cannot deliver the full design. It can deliver the first parts and prove the approach. The full design needs several teams, with child protection run by its own team from the start, as the architecture intends.
timeline › plans › e › assumptions › 1: Procurement lead times are planning assumptions, not figures from the research. We assume 4 to 9 months for a large competitive purchase, and 2 to 4 months when an existing agreement or standing offer can be used.
timeline › plans › e › assumptions › 2: We count the whole team of 12 as delivery capacity: 12 people times 220 working days is 2,640 person-days a year. That is generous, because the director and product manager will not build software.
timeline › plans › e › assumptions › 3: Effort is built from rough rules of thumb in the technology and payments research, which the authors call a floor, plus figures borrowed from the SaaS CRM research for the parts the floor leaves out. Treat it as a low estimate.
timeline › plans › e › assumptions › 4: This plan moves a thin, read-only worker view ahead of the full shared foundations. The target architecture's own order builds all foundations first and puts the first visible release at 18 to 27 months. Only read-only pieces can safely move earlier, because they cannot damage ICM's records.
timeline › plans › e › assumptions › 5: The first release reads a copy of changes from ICM's database. Oracle's written position on doing that continuously from the live database is needed first.
timeline › plans › e › assumptions › 6: Free software runs on the government's own private cloud, an existing service. The event stream software (Kafka) is not yet on that platform's supported list. We assume the platform team supports the pilot, and that support is confirmed in writing before the new system becomes the official record for anything.
timeline › plans › e › assumptions › 7: Changes inside ICM must go through the team that configures it, on its monthly release cycle. Its time must be booked ahead.
timeline › plans › e › assumptions › 8: The order of programs follows the target architecture: smallest set of rules and lowest harm first, employment assistance late, child protection last.
timeline › plans › e › assumptions › 9: Payment work assumes the Comptroller General's office accepts a new ministry payment system, as provincial policy requires. The bank's file format is also not confirmed.
timeline › plans › e › assumptions › 10: Payments for a program go live only after side-by-side runs show zero difference for three monthly cycles, as the architecture requires.
timeline › plans › e › assumptions › 11: The team needs skills it may not have, such as recording facts with several dates and running the event stream. The architecture names the first as the biggest skills gap in the program.
timeline › plans › e › assumptions › 12: Child protection estimates have not had a second reader, so they may grow.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 1 › name: Discovery and setup
timeline › plans › e › phases › 1 › goal: Learn how the work is done today, and set up hosting on the government's own private cloud.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 2 › name: Shared foundations, built in thin layers
timeline › plans › e › phases › 2 › goal: Build only the shared parts the next release needs: the event stream, the evidence store, the ministry's own data rules for other systems, and the link layer to ICM.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 3 › name: First release: a better worker view
timeline › plans › e › phases › 3 › goal: Give workers a fast client search and one summary across programs, without writing anything back to ICM.

timeline › plans › e › phases › 3 › releases › 1 › who: Workers in one office
timeline › plans › e › phases › 3 › releases › 1 › what: Search for a client and see one summary across programs. It reads a copy of ICM's changes and writes nothing, so it cannot damage ICM's records.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 3 › releases › 2 › name: All offices
timeline › plans › e › phases › 3 › releases › 2 › who: Workers in every office
timeline › plans › e › phases › 3 › releases › 2 › what: The same search and summary, with fixes from the pilot.

timeline › plans › e › phases › 3 › releases › 3 › what: Likely duplicate client records are flagged for a person to decide. Merges are recorded so they can be undone.

timeline › plans › e › phases › 4 › goal: Make letters in the new system, tie each one to its decision, and switch off ICM's letters. This is the first part of ICM to be retired.

timeline › plans › e › phases › 5 › releases › 5 › what: A group of applications is moved back to ICM and forward again for real, to prove it can be done if something goes wrong.

timeline › plans › e › phases › 8 › name: Payments and overpayments
timeline › plans › e › phases › 8 › goal: Pay clients of the moved programs through one payment service with its own ledger, matched every day to the bank and the government's accounts.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 8 › releases › 1 › name: Side-by-side payment runs
timeline › plans › e › phases › 8 › releases › 1 › who: Finance staff
timeline › plans › e › phases › 8 › releases › 1 › what: The new payment run works out each payment next to the old one. It must match to the cent for three monthly cycles.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 8 › releases › 2 › name: First live payment run
timeline › plans › e › phases › 8 › releases › 2 › who: Child care subsidy and employment services clients

timeline › plans › e › phases › 8 › releases › 3 › name: Overpayments and debts
timeline › plans › e › phases › 8 › releases › 3 › who: Finance and recovery staff
timeline › plans › e › phases › 8 › releases › 3 › what: Overpayments are raised, repaid, written off or sent to collections in the new system.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 8 › releases › 4 › name: Emergency payments tested
timeline › plans › e › phases › 8 › releases › 4 › who: Finance and operations staff
timeline › plans › e › phases › 8 › releases › 4 › what: The emergency payment path is run for real in a test, not just written down.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 8 › releases › 5 › name: Old payment path switched off
timeline › plans › e › phases › 8 › releases › 5 › who: Finance staff
timeline › plans › e › phases › 8 › releases › 5 › what: The old payment path for these programs is turned off.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 9 › name: Reviews and appeals
timeline › plans › e › phases › 9 › goal: Handle reviews and appeals once, for every program, with their legal deadlines.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 9 › releases › 1 › name: Reviews and appeals
timeline › plans › e › phases › 9 › releases › 1 › who: Clients asking for a review, and the staff who handle it
timeline › plans › e › phases › 9 › releases › 1 › what: Reviews and appeals run in the new system for every program moved so far. A successful appeal is paid through the same payment service.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 10 › name: Disability assistance and employment assistance
timeline › plans › e › phases › 10 › goal: Move the two largest programs together, last among the adult programs, because a wrong answer here can mean someone cannot buy food this month.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 10 › releases › 1 › name: Side-by-side decisions
timeline › plans › e › phases › 10 › releases › 1 › who: Program staff
timeline › plans › e › phases › 10 › releases › 1 › what: The new rules work out disability and employment assistance for real cases next to ICM for three monthly cycles.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 10 › releases › 2 › name: First region moves
timeline › plans › e › phases › 10 › releases › 2 › who: Clients and workers in one region
timeline › plans › e › phases › 10 › releases › 2 › what: Decisions and payments for both programs move together, because the disability decision sets the rate employment assistance pays.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 10 › releases › 3 › name: More regions

timeline › plans › e › phases › 10 › releases › 4 › who: Clients and workers in about half the province
timeline › plans › e › phases › 10 › releases › 4 › what: More regions move in groups.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 10 › releases › 5 › name: Rest of the province
timeline › plans › e › phases › 10 › releases › 5 › who: All remaining clients and workers in both programs
timeline › plans › e › phases › 10 › releases › 5 › what: The rest of the caseload moves.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 10 › releases › 6 › name: Old decision paths switched off
timeline › plans › e › phases › 10 › releases › 6 › who: Program staff
timeline › plans › e › phases › 10 › releases › 6 › what: ICM's decision paths for both programs are turned off.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › name: Child protection
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › goal: Move child protection last, with its own design work and permission to build rather than configure, because it has the least structured practice and the strictest privacy needs.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 1 › name: Caregivers and providers
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 1 › who: Foster caregivers, service providers and the workers who support them
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 1 › what: Caregiver and provider records move to the new system.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 2 › name: Family plans and agreements
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 2 › who: Child protection workers
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 2 › what: Care plans and agreements with families are made and tracked in the new system.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 3 › name: Court documents
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 3 › who: Child protection workers who go to court
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 3 › what: Court proceedings, orders and their documents are tracked in the new system.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 4 › name: Reports of concern
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 4 › who: The 24/7 reporting line and intake workers
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 4 › what: Calls about a child's safety go straight into the case, on the ministry's own release calendar.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 5 › name: Investigations
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 5 › who: Child protection workers
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 5 › what: Investigations and safety assessments are done in the new system.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 6 › name: Adoption
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 6 › who: Adoption workers
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 6 › what: Adoption records move to the new system.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 7 › name: Remaining cases move
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 7 › who: All child protection workers
timeline › plans › e › phases › 11 › releases › 7 › what: The rest of the open child protection cases move from ICM in groups.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 12 › name: Move the remaining history
timeline › plans › e › phases › 12 › goal: Move closed cases and old records out of ICM with their original dates, and check that every record arrived.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 12 › releases › 1 › name: History check complete
timeline › plans › e › phases › 12 › releases › 1 › who: Records staff and auditors
timeline › plans › e › phases › 12 › releases › 1 › what: Every old record is in the new system or in a checked archive, with its original dates.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 13 › name: Switch off ICM
timeline › plans › e › phases › 13 › goal: Turn off what is left of ICM and the Siebel product it runs on, close its last links, and keep a controlled archive.
timeline › plans › e › phases › 13 › releases › 1 › name: ICM switched off
timeline › plans › e › phases › 13 › releases › 1 › who: Everyone
timeline › plans › e › phases › 13 › releases › 1 › what: ICM is turned off. Its licence, support and servers stop costing money.
timeline › plans › e › procurement › 1 › item: Support contract for the event stream software (Apache Kafka), only if the government's private cloud team cannot support it
timeline › plans › e › procurement › 1 › why: The event stream carries every fact and decision between the parts. The software is free, but someone must be on call when it breaks.
timeline › plans › e › procurement › 1 › startBy: Month 1
timeline › plans › e › procurement › 2 › item: Electronic signature service
timeline › plans › e › procurement › 2 › why: Clients and workers need to sign forms online. The research suggests asking OneSpan. The ministry already uses DocuSign elsewhere.
timeline › plans › e › procurement › 2 › startBy: By month 22
timeline › plans › e › procurement › 3 › item: Document scanning and capture tool, only if government services do not cover it
timeline › plans › e › procurement › 3 › why: Paper and uploaded documents must be scanned, read and filed against the right case. The research says buy or adopt this, not build it.
timeline › plans › e › procurement › 3 › startBy: By month 20
timeline › plans › e › procurement › 4 › item: Price quote for a commercial rules-writing tool (GoRules' paid product)
timeline › plans › e › procurement › 4 › why: The plan builds rule-writing tools around a free rules engine. The rules engine decision needs a priced commercial option to compare. If the paid tool wins, it becomes a purchase.
timeline › plans › e › procurement › 4 › startBy: By month 44
timeline › plans › e › procurement › 5 › item: Account matching (reconciliation) product, only if the ministry decides to buy rather than build
timeline › plans › e › procurement › 5 › why: Matches the ministry's ledger with the bank and the government's accounts every day. It is the one payments part where buying is plausible. A request for information is drafted but not sent.
timeline › plans › e › procurement › 5 › startBy: By month 56
timeline › team › 1 › role: Developers
timeline › team › 1 › count: 6 to 9
timeline › team › 1 › focus: Build, test and release the system. On the SaaS CRM plans they need CRM and integration platform skills. On the event-driven plan they need skills in the open-source parts and in recording facts with their dates.
timeline › team › 2 › role: UX designers
timeline › team › 2 › count: 1 to 2
timeline › team › 2 › focus: Design the screens and online forms. Test them with workers and clients, including people who use screen readers.
timeline › team › 3 › role: Service designer
timeline › team › 3 › focus: Map how the work really happens across workers, clients and partners. Plan how each program moves to the new system, one group at a time.
timeline › team › 4 › role: Product manager
timeline › team › 4 › focus: Decide what goes into each release and in what order. Keep the list of work tied to what workers and clients need most.
timeline › team › 5 › role: Director
timeline › team › 5 › focus: Lead the team. Get the funding, decisions and purchases each release needs, and report progress to ministry leaders.

, in
A plain-language guide to three options for replacing ICM. It draws on the project's research. Nothing here is a government decision or commitment.
A release
Already in government
An open question or risk to manage
Anything bought from a company goes through government procurement. Work that needs it can't start until it lands.
Build or buy
Cannot be met
Dig below the surface
Done, but in a weaker way
Draft for discussion
Each option deals with these root causes in a different way. See what each one would change.
Each plan puts something real in front of staff or clients as early as it can, then releases on a steady beat. That can make the whole project longer. It also means less risk and sooner benefits.
